instructions.knownIssuesMd:
## Known Issues

- Nested modals do not work on iOS; switch views inside one modal instead.
- Lending goes through /api/loans rather than Firestore directly, because the security rules for `loans` are incomplete.

security.authMethod: Firebase Auth — Google and Apple sign-in, email/password on web
security.dataEncryption: In transit by the provider; Firestore encrypts at rest

components.name: Web app
components.oneLiner: The main reading tracker.
components.notes: Stripe for subscriptions — web only, never iOS.

components.name: iOS app
components.oneLiner: Barcode scanning, reading timer, offline library.
components.notes: Apple IAP for Pro; Sign in with Apple is required by App Store review.

components.name: Home screen widgets
components.oneLiner: Small, medium and large widgets showing reading stats.
components.notes: Reads stats through App Group group.io.librora.app.

components.name: Reading timer Live Activity
components.oneLiner: Dynamic Island and lock screen timer.
components.notes: iOS 16.2+. Bridged from JS via LiveActivityModule.swift.

components.name: Shared core
components.oneLiner: Types, Zod schemas, subscription limits, ISBN utilities.
components.notes: Imported by both web and mobile as @librora/core.

decisions.title: Database
decisions.rationale: The mobile app has to work with no signal — on a train, in a library basement. Firestore gives offline persistence and conflict resolution without writing a sync layer, which for a two-platform product built by one person is the whole argument.
decisions.alternatives: Postgres with a hand-written sync layer. Cheaper per read and far better at the reporting the Insights page wants, but offline sync is months of work and the hardest kind to get right.
decisions.tradeoffs: Queries are weak: anything resembling a join or an aggregate is assembled client-side. Reads are billed, so a careless listener is a bill. Pagination for getMyBooks is still deferred because the Firestore half is easy and the virtualised list is not.

decisions.title: Shared logic
decisions.rationale: Subscription limits, ISBN validation and category lists have to agree exactly between web and mobile, and the cost of them disagreeing is a user charged wrongly or a book filed twice. No React and no Firebase in it, so both platforms can import it and it can be tested on its own.
decisions.alternatives: Duplicating the rules in each app, which is what happens by default and drifts within weeks.
decisions.tradeoffs: A monorepo and its hoisting problems: the root must pin react and react-dom to 18 or the Next build breaks, because mobile is on 19.

decisions.title: Payments
decisions.choice: Stripe on web, Apple IAP on iOS
decisions.rationale: Not a preference — Apple requires in-app purchase for digital features and rejects anything that routes around it. Stripe stays on web where the fee is lower and the flow is ours.
decisions.alternatives: None available. Stripe-only would fail review.
decisions.tradeoffs: Two payment systems, two sets of webhooks, two definitions of entitlement that have to resolve to the same answer.

decisions.title: Widgets and Live Activities in Swift
decisions.rationale: WidgetKit and ActivityKit have no React Native equivalent. The timer on the lock screen and the Dynamic Island are platform features, and reaching them means native code — there is no decision to make beyond accepting it.
decisions.alternatives: Third-party bridges, which lag each iOS release.
decisions.tradeoffs: A second language in the repository, an App Group to pass data across, and native modules needing a dev client rebuild before anyone can test them.

risks.title: Firestore rules for loans are incomplete
risks.detail: Mobile lending writes through /api/loans instead of Firestore directly, specifically because the security rules for the loans collection do not cover it. The API is a workaround for a gap that is still open underneath.
risks.mitigation: Write the rules, then move the mobile client back onto Firestore directly and delete the endpoint.

risks.title: Unauthenticated public endpoints have no rate limit
risks.detail: /api/isbn-lookup and /api/google-books are public and unauthenticated. The Google Books key allows 1,000 requests a day and is shared by everyone.
risks.mitigation: Upstash Redis for shared state across Vercel instances. It must not block iOS, which calls these legitimately.

risks.title: OCR runs on a public demo key
risks.detail: OCR_SPACE_API_KEY is not set, so photo scan falls back to the key printed in OCR.space documentation and shared with everyone who copied it. Its quota is spent by strangers and can run out at any moment.
risks.mitigation: Register at ocr.space — free, email only — and set the key in Vercel and .env.local.

risks.title: Old Chronos collections never deleted
risks.detail: The migration on 2026-08-20 left users/{uid}/philosophers and users/{uid}/chronos_authors in place as a backup. They have been read by nothing since.
risks.mitigation: Delete per user in the Firebase console once the unified authors have been confirmed correct in production.

risks.title: Next.js 14 while 15 is out
risks.detail: No known blockers, but a major upgrade needs a dedicated testing pass and nothing is broken today.
risks.mitigation: Schedule it as its own piece of work rather than attaching it to a feature.

costs.notes: Required to ship on the App Store at all.
Price not recorded — check the Name.com invoice.
Hobby is free; Pro is 20/month. Which one is in use is not recorded here.
Firestore reads and storage. Spark is free with quotas; Blaze is pay-as-you-go.
1,000 requests a day.
25,000 a month, capped at 500 a day per IP — shared by the whole user base because calls leave from the server.

instructions.localSetupMd:
## Local Setup

```bash
npm install
npx prisma generate
npm run dev
```

The dev server caches the Prisma client in memory: after `prisma generate` it must be restarted, and a second server on port 3000 will serve a stale one.
instructions.deployMd:
## Deployment

Vercel, on push to `main`. The build runs `prisma migrate deploy` before `next build`, so a successful deployment implies the migration applied.

Commits must be authored as the Vercel account owner or the deployment sits in BLOCKED with no explanation in the CLI output.
instructions.testingMd:
## Testing

```bash
npx vitest run
```

250+ tests. The field matcher for the extension is tested against the markup real ATS systems emit, including the negative cases — filling a referrer field with your own name is worse than filling nothing.
instructions.knownIssuesMd:
## Known Issues

- `prisma migrate dev` wants a database reset because `rate_limits` is created lazily at runtime by design. Migrations are written by hand and applied with `$executeRawUnsafe`, then marked with `prisma migrate resolve --applied`.
- Sign-up is not restricted: anyone with the URL can create an account.

security.authMethod: Better Auth, Google OAuth only; email/password disabled
security.dataEncryption: OAuth tokens encrypted with the auth secret before they reach Postgres
security.complianceNotes: Holds a full job search including contacts and documents. The extension token is hashed; it is shown once and cannot be read back.

decisions.title: Database
decisions.rationale: The product is relational to its core — applications, stages, interviews, contacts, documents — and the analytics are the point. A funnel that must say "rejected at assignment" without claiming a conversion needs joins and real constraints.
decisions.alternatives: Firestore, as used in Librora. Rejected because every report would be assembled in memory and the stage model could not be enforced.
decisions.tradeoffs: No offline story, which is fine for a web app. Migrations are written by hand here because `migrate dev` wants a reset.

decisions.title: Status model
decisions.choice: Four separate fields: stage, milestones, history, outcome
decisions.rationale: A search goes interview, then assignment, then interview again. One status field cannot express "back at interviewing, having already done the assignment", and collapsing offer into hired would make the funnel claim conversions that never happened.
decisions.alternatives: A single status enum, which is what every tracker starts with and why none of them can answer that question.
decisions.tradeoffs: More to keep consistent, and a UI that had to be redesigned to show one control over two fields.

decisions.title: Generated documents are verified, not trusted
decisions.rationale: A tailored resume is read for fit, not fact-checked line by line, so an invented employer or a stretched date survives all the way to an interview. The prompt asks for good behaviour; the verifier enforces it and refuses to save a document that invents.
decisions.alternatives: Trusting the model, which fails silently and exactly where it is most expensive.
decisions.tradeoffs: A whole verification layer, and occasional refusals on documents that were fine.

decisions.title: No mailbox connection
decisions.rationale: Reading a mailbox needs restricted Gmail scopes and a CASA assessment, for a feature that pasting solves in one keystroke. The clipboard HTML even keeps the links, which is what the parser actually needs.
decisions.tradeoffs: Nothing happens automatically; the person has to paste.

decisions.title: Extension reaches pages through activeTab
decisions.rationale: Employers host the application form on their own domain, so a host list cannot cover them. activeTab grants one tab for one press and expires by itself, which gets the capability without standing permission to read every page.
decisions.alternatives: <all_urls>, which would work everywhere and ask for far more than it needs.
decisions.tradeoffs: A press is required on sites outside the list.

risks.title: Sign-up is open to anyone with the URL
risks.detail: There is no allowlist on sign-in — only on the admin area. Any Google account can create a tracker, and that data lands in the same Neon database under a privacy policy that describes a tool for one person.
risks.mitigation: An allowlist on sign-in, in the shape already used for admin. Needed before the extension link is shared.

risks.title: One Anthropic key shared with Chronos
risks.detail: The same ANTHROPIC_API_KEY serves this project and Chronos. Rotating or revoking it breaks both, and the rate limits are shared, so a busy sweep here degrades Chronos.
risks.mitigation: Separate keys per project. Deliberate for now.

risks.title: Preview deployments lack the AI key
risks.detail: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set for Production and Development but not Preview, so every AI path fails on a preview deployment with an inline message rather than an obvious error.
risks.mitigation: Set it through the Vercel REST API — the CLI cannot add Preview variables on this account.

risks.title: Holds an entire job search
risks.detail: Applications, correspondence, contacts, uploaded documents and a full CV. A breach would expose a job search to a current employer.
risks.mitigation: Extension tokens are hashed and shown once; OAuth tokens are encrypted before storage. The open sign-up above is the weak point.

costs.notes: Paid 2026-11-23. One-off, covers the account rather than the item.
Free tier is likely; not verified.
Same account as Librora.

projects.oneLiner: Feel. Track. Understand. — privacy-first mood, cycle and context analytics.

instructions.localSetupMd:
## Local Setup

Node 24 is pinned for this project through fnm and `.nvmrc`; the global Node is untouched.

```bash
fnm exec --using=24 pnpm install
```
instructions.deployMd:
## Deployment

Firebase Hosting for the client, Firebase Functions for the backend.

The iOS build goes through Capacitor and Xcode.

operations.secretsLocation: Firebase project config; see notenv-style local files

security.dataEncryption: On-device SQLite for the sensitive records; Firestore encrypts at rest
security.complianceNotes: Holds menstrual cycle and mood data — among the most sensitive categories there are. Privacy-first is the product claim, so anything that moves data off the device needs a deliberate decision.

decisions.title: Framework
decisions.rationale: The only project here not on React, and deliberately: it is the stack worked in daily, so the product moves fastest and the habits are already right.
decisions.alternatives: React, used by everything else in this portfolio.
decisions.tradeoffs: Nothing is shared with the other projects — no common components, no common utilities.

decisions.title: iOS through Capacitor rather than React Native
decisions.rationale: The client is already an Angular web app. Capacitor ships that same app as a native shell, so one codebase covers both without rewriting the UI.
decisions.alternatives: A separate React Native app, which would mean maintaining the product twice.
decisions.tradeoffs: Native feel is limited by what the web view gives. Platform features need plugins.

decisions.title: Sensitive data stored on the device
decisions.rationale: Mood and menstrual cycle records are among the most sensitive categories there are. Privacy-first is the product claim, and the strongest form of it is data that never leaves the phone.
decisions.alternatives: Firestore for everything, which is simpler and makes the claim untrue.
decisions.tradeoffs: No sync between devices, no server-side analysis, and a backup story that has to be built rather than inherited.

risks.title: A flaw in the crypto design or its implementation
risks.detail: Risk R-01 in docs/DECISIONS.md. The product’s promise is that mood and cycle data stay private; a mistake here voids it silently.
risks.mitigation: Standard primitives only, test vectors, a written threat model, and an independent review gate at Phase 9.

risks.title: Losing the key loses the history
risks.detail: Risk R-02. Encrypted data with no key is gone.
risks.mitigation: Recovery-key confirmation, backups, device linking, an iCloud Keychain option.

risks.title: Sync conflicts could drop entries without saying so
risks.detail: Risk R-03 and R-25. Sync is hand-written on Firestore with a sequence counter and transactions, which is easier to get wrong than SQL.
risks.mitigation: Field-level HLC merge keeping conflicts, a never-delete-on-conflict rule, one transactional syncPush function, and multi-device property tests.

risks.title: Google could suspend the project
risks.detail: Risk R-22. Auth, sync and the proxies all sit on one Firebase project; losing it takes them down together.
risks.mitigation: The core app works offline, clients keep full local copies and an encrypted export, billing alerts are set, and SyncBackend / AuthProvider adapters give a documented migration path.

risks.title: The weather proxy limit is per IP
risks.detail: Risk R-26: 120 requests an hour per IP. Users behind carrier-grade NAT share one, and bulk history imports hit it — seen in Phase 5 verification as 429s leaving jobs pending.
risks.mitigation: Client-side cache of fetched hours per cell, so only missing hours are requested. A per-account quota was rejected because it would link identity to coordinates.

risks.title: Nine phases is more than gets finished
risks.detail: Risk R-15. A half-built feature with visible controls is worse than an absent one.
risks.mitigation: Feature flags hide unfinished work — no fake controls — with a checklist and definition-of-done gating each phase.

risks.title: Statistically misleading insights
risks.detail: Risk R-08. The app correlates mood with weather, cycle and context; naive correlation on this data produces confident nonsense about a person’s health.
risks.mitigation: Conservative thresholds, false-discovery-rate control, day-level units, explicit "exploratory" labels, and a stats review.

costs.notes: No extra cost — the existing Librora membership covers it ($99/yr).
About $3.80 a month. DNS on Vercel nameservers.

costs.item: WeatherKit and Apple Maps Server API
costs.notes: Included with the membership; WeatherKit allows 500k calls a month.
Email, Google and Apple sign-in are free.
About 2M invocations a month free, then roughly $0.40 per million. Blaze needs a card on file.
Within the free daily quota (~50k reads, 20k writes, 1 GiB).

registrations.name: Firebase project
registrations.notes: Separate project and billing budget from Librora, deliberately (R-21). $5 budget alert set at creation.

security.complianceNotes: Holds reading history rather than identifying data.

decisions.title: Lives in the Librora monorepo but deploys separately
decisions.rationale: It shares types and Firebase configuration with Librora, so a separate repository would mean copying both. A separate Vercel project keeps the deployments independent, so a Chronos build cannot break librora.io.
decisions.alternatives: Its own repository, or a route inside the Librora web app.
decisions.tradeoffs: The monorepo root has to satisfy both, which is where the React 18/19 pinning comes from.

decisions.title: Maps without a keyed provider
decisions.rationale: The geography view needed to exist before anyone knew whether it would be used. Nominatim and OSM need no key, no billing account and no quota negotiation, so the feature could ship and be judged.
decisions.alternatives: Google Maps or Mapbox — better data, but a key, a card and a per-view price for a feature that might be removed.
decisions.tradeoffs: Nominatim asks for polite use and is not built for volume. Real traffic means moving to a keyed provider.

risks.title: Old collections still in Firestore
risks.detail: philosophers and chronos_authors were left after the 2026-08-20 migration as a backup and nothing reads them.
risks.mitigation: Delete per user once production is confirmed correct.

risks.title: Deprecated photoUrl still read by the UI
risks.detail: The Author type keeps photoUrl for backward compatibility and three components still read it instead of photos[0].
risks.mitigation: Move them to photos[0] after the old collections are gone.

risks.title: Nominatim has no quota guarantee
risks.detail: A free public service with a usage policy rather than a contract. It can rate-limit or block at any time.
risks.mitigation: Acceptable while usage is one person. A keyed provider before that changes.

costs.notes: A subdomain of librora.io — no separate cost, and it lapses when that domain does.
A second project on the same account.
Shared key with Job Tracker.

projects.name: Vesper
projects.oneLiner: A private life OS. Everything encrypted in the browser before it leaves.
projects.essence: A single person’s map of goals, plans, timeline, boards and finances. The server never sees plaintext: records and images are sealed with AES-256-GCM in the browser, under a key wrapped by a passphrase (Argon2id) and by a recovery key. Firestore holds ciphertext only.

components.oneLiner: Map, overview, plan, goals, timeline, boards, finance, analytics, settings.

components.name: Crypto layer
components.oneLiner: AES-GCM, the keyring (Argon2id / HKDF, wrap and unwrap), the device key.

components.oneLiner: SSRF-safe image download and optional entry translation. Both verify the ID token.

instructions.localSetupMd:
## Local Setup

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

decisions.title: Where decryption happens
decisions.choice: In the browser, never on the server
decisions.rationale: The vault is the point. If the server could read a record, a subpoena, a misconfigured rule or a bad deploy could too. Keeping the key in the browser means the hosting provider and the database are untrusted by design.
decisions.tradeoffs: No server-side search, no server-side rendering of content, and analytics have to run on the client over decrypted data.

decisions.title: How the key is protected
decisions.choice: Argon2id at 64 MiB, t=3, with a random data key wrapped twice
decisions.rationale: A passphrase alone is guessable; a random 256-bit data key is not. The passphrase and the recovery key each wrap the same data key, so changing the passphrase does not re-encrypt the vault.
decisions.tradeoffs: 64 MiB of memory per unlock is noticeable on a phone. OWASP’s baseline is 19 MiB; Firestore rules reject keyrings below it.

decisions.title: Fetching images from a link
decisions.choice: A server route that verifies the token and blocks internal addresses
decisions.rationale: Images have to be downloaded once and stored encrypted, which the browser cannot do across origins. A naive proxy is an SSRF hole into Vercel’s network.
decisions.tradeoffs: One route that must stay correct; it is the only place the server touches a URL the user supplied.

decisions.title: Translation is optional and off
decisions.choice: Anthropic API, only when switched on
decisions.rationale: Sending entry text to a model is the one thing that breaks the privacy promise, so it is a setting the owner turns on knowingly rather than a default.
decisions.tradeoffs: Without the key the app costs nothing and translation is simply absent.

risks.title: Losing the key loses everything
risks.detail: Nobody can decrypt the vault without the passphrase or the recovery key — not the owner, not the host, not a support process, because none exists.
risks.mitigation: A 52-character recovery key, shown and confirmed at setup, with lenient parsing. Recovery and rotation documented in docs/RECOVERY.md.

risks.title: A flaw in the crypto code
risks.detail: Hand-assembled key handling is where this class of product fails, and a mistake is silent.
risks.mitigation: Standard primitives only, from Web Crypto, with Argon2id from hash-wasm. Non-extractable CryptoKey; raw bytes zeroed after use. Threat model in docs/SECURITY.md.

risks.title: The image route reaches the network on request
risks.detail: A route that fetches a user-supplied URL can be pointed at internal services.
risks.mitigation: ID token verified with jose, allowlist checked in Firestore, SSRF-safe download.

risks.title: Keyring strength is enforced in rules, not only in code
risks.detail: A client could write a keyring derived with weak parameters.
risks.mitigation: Firestore rules reject keyrings below OWASP’s baseline of 19 MiB and t=2.

risks.title: Translation sends text to a third party
risks.detail: With translation on, the text of an entry leaves the device in plaintext to Anthropic.
risks.mitigation: Off by default, documented in docs/AI_PRIVACY.md, and only the entry text is sent.

costs.notes: Pages plus three small API routes.
One user.
Under 5 MB stored; a few hundred reads per unlock.
Only with translation on: about $0.50 a month at 100 edits; a one-off full-plan translation is $0.40–0.60. Zero without the key.

portfolio.fullDescription: A personal system for structuring life areas, goals and routines. Early — twelve commits in, the shape is still being decided.

projects.name: DojoDash
projects.oneLiner: Kids sports club management — attendance, medals, groups and families.
projects.essence: A club management platform with three roles: admin, coach and family. Coaches take attendance and award medals; families manage their children and see progress. XP, levels, streaks and group leaderboards sit on top of attendance.

frontend.name: Next.js
frontend.notes: App Router, TypeScript, Mantine v7, TanStack Query

backend.name: Firebase Cloud Functions
backend.notes: Callable functions per role, plus Firestore triggers

hosting.name: Vercel
hosting.notes: Web app; Firebase hosts rules, functions and storage

auth.name: Firebase Auth
auth.notes: Roles as custom claims: admin, coach, family

components.name: Web app
components.oneLiner: The whole product — admin, coach and family areas.

components.name: Mobile app
components.oneLiner: Expo client. Scaffolded, not released.

components.name: Cloud Functions
components.oneLiner: Callable functions for admin and coach actions, and Firestore triggers.

components.name: Shared packages
components.oneLiner: core (domain logic, Zod schemas), firebase (DAL), ui (Mantine theme), club, config.

decisions.title: Domain logic in a platform-agnostic package
decisions.rationale: XP, streaks and leaderboard maths are the part most likely to be wanted on a phone as well as on the web. Keeping them free of React and Firebase means the Expo app can use them unchanged.
decisions.tradeoffs: One more package to version, and the temptation to put Firebase types in it has to be resisted.

decisions.title: A component library rather than hand-rolled UI
decisions.rationale: The product is forms and tables — attendance, groups, users. Mantine ships both, with dates and notifications, so the work goes into club rules instead of into a date picker.
decisions.tradeoffs: The look is Mantine’s; escaping it later means rewriting the surface.

decisions.title: Bot protection on a product used by children
decisions.choice: Firebase App Check with reCAPTCHA v3
decisions.rationale: Registration is open to families, so the sign-up path is exposed. App Check rejects calls that did not come from the real app before they reach Firestore or a function.
decisions.tradeoffs: A failing App Check locks out legitimate users, and the failure mode is opaque.

decisions.title: Privacy defaults chosen against the product’s interest
decisions.choice: Full name and photo off by default
decisions.rationale: The data belongs to minors. A leaderboard is more engaging with faces and full names, which is exactly why the parent has to turn them on rather than find them already on.
decisions.tradeoffs: Leaderboards look emptier until parents opt in, and most never will.

risks.title: The product holds data about children
risks.detail: Names, photos, dates of birth and attendance of minors. Coaches see full names for attendance; parent contact details and dates of birth are kept from them.
risks.mitigation: Per-child privacy settings controlled by the parent, defaulting to first name only and no photo. Documented in docs/privacy-notes.md.

risks.title: Roles live in custom claims
risks.detail: Admin, coach and family are Firebase custom claims. A claim set wrongly, or a stale token after a role change, grants access the security rules will honour.
risks.mitigation: Claims are only written by admin callable functions; rules check them on every read. A forced token refresh after a role change is not yet verified.

risks.title: No production Firebase project yet
risks.detail: docs/deployment.md describes creating dojodash-prod; development runs against emulators and dojodash-dev.
risks.mitigation: Deployment guide is written; the project has to be created and App Check keys issued before real families use it.

risks.title: Free Firebase quotas are shared by the whole club
risks.detail: Attendance writes and leaderboard reads scale with children times sessions, against a daily free quota.
risks.mitigation: Small at club scale. Budget alerts before opening it to more than one club.

costs.notes: Within the free tier.
Functions need Blaze before production.

projects.name: J.O.C.A.S.T.A.
projects.oneLiner: AI scheduling assistant that plans around travel time and weather.
projects.essence: Type "pick up groceries at Costco tomorrow" and get a scheduling proposal. Syncs both ways with Google Calendar without duplicating events, works out travel time between them with traffic and weather, and asks for confirmation through Telegram with inline buttons.

frontend.name: Expo / React Native
frontend.notes: Expo Router + Tamagui; one codebase for iOS and web

hosting.name: Vercel + Render
hosting.notes: Web on Vercel, API on Render (free plan)

auth.name: Google OAuth + JWT
auth.notes: Calendar scopes; refresh tokens encrypted at rest

components.name: Client (iOS + web)
components.oneLiner: Expo Router app that also builds for the web.

components.name: API server
components.oneLiner: NestJS API: scheduling, calendar sync, travel and weather.

components.name: Telegram bot
components.oneLiner: Notifications with Accept / Snooze / Reschedule buttons.

components.name: Shared package
components.oneLiner: Types, Zod schemas and utilities used by both apps.

decisions.title: The model never runs on the device
decisions.rationale: Natural-language extraction needs a key, and a key in a React Native bundle is a published key. The server holds it and the client sends text.
decisions.tradeoffs: Nothing works offline, and every parse is a round trip.

decisions.title: Calendar sync has to survive being run twice
decisions.choice: Bi-directional sync keyed on event identity
decisions.rationale: A scheduling assistant that duplicates events on every sync is worse than no assistant. Identity is matched rather than appended to.
decisions.tradeoffs: Matching rules are the part most likely to be subtly wrong, and the failure is silent.

decisions.title: Travel time is part of the schedule, not a note on it
decisions.choice: Google Directions + Open-Meteo, per transport mode
decisions.rationale: The point of the product is that an event at 3pm across town is not free. Sedan, motorcycle, taxi and transit are weighted differently, and Calgary weather changes the motorcycle and transit numbers.
decisions.tradeoffs: Two more external APIs in the critical path, each with its own quota.

decisions.title: The API runs on a free plan
decisions.rationale: A personal assistant with one user does not justify paying for an always-on server.
decisions.tradeoffs: The instance sleeps and can be reclaimed. As of 2026-11-24 the API does not answer at all, while the web app does.

risks.title: The API is not responding
risks.detail: https://jocasta-api.onrender.com returned nothing on 2026-11-24, while the web app at jocasta-io.vercel.app answered 200. Render reclaims free instances.
risks.mitigation: Redeploy from render.yaml, or move the API to a plan that stays awake.

risks.title: Google OAuth is unverified
risks.detail: Users see "Google hasn’t verified this app". Calendar scopes are sensitive, so verification needs a privacy policy, terms and a logo.
risks.mitigation: Steps written up in GoogleVerification.md; the privacy and terms pages have to be deployed first.

risks.title: Google refresh tokens are held by the server
risks.detail: The API stores long-lived Google credentials that grant calendar access.
risks.mitigation: Encrypted with ENCRYPTION_KEY; JWT access and refresh secrets kept separate. Key rotation is not documented.

risks.title: Every parse costs money
risks.detail: Natural-language input calls OpenAI on each submission, and Directions is billed per request.
risks.mitigation: GPT-4o-mini is the cheap model; usage is one person.

costs.notes: Sleeps when idle; currently not answering.

projects.name: Company Portal
projects.oneLiner: Multi-tenant HR platform: timesheets, requests, documents.
projects.essence: A SaaS HR portal with five roles — employee, manager, HR admin, tenant admin, platform operator. Tenants share one database and are kept apart by row-level security, with a documented path to heavier isolation if the tenant count demands it.

database.name: PostgreSQL
database.notes: Shared database, row-level security per tenant

auth.name: Auth0
auth.notes: Behind an abstraction layer; WorkOS is the intended successor

components.name: Web app
components.oneLiner: Employee, manager and HR surfaces.

components.name: API server
components.oneLiner: NestJS, tenant middleware, row-level security.

components.name: Admin panel
components.oneLiner: Platform operator surface across tenants.

components.name: iOS app
components.oneLiner: Planned, not started. Scoped in docs/MOBILE_FUTURE.md.

decisions.title: How tenants are kept apart
decisions.rationale: Under a hundred tenants, a schema or database per tenant buys isolation at the price of migrations, connection pooling and backup complexity that a product with no customers yet cannot afford to carry.
decisions.alternatives: Schema per tenant (10–1000 tenants); database per tenant (enterprise, compliance).
decisions.tradeoffs: A noisy tenant affects the rest, and one database is one thing to lose. Every query depends on the tenant middleware being right.

decisions.title: The identity provider is behind a seam
decisions.choice: Auth abstraction layer with an Auth0 adapter
decisions.rationale: Auth0 is what it uses now and WorkOS is where it is meant to go. Writing the adapter first makes that a change of one module rather than of every route.
decisions.tradeoffs: An abstraction over exactly one implementation is a guess about the second one.

decisions.title: Files are not in the database
decisions.rationale: HR documents are large, numerous and rarely read. Keeping them out of Postgres keeps backups and restores to a size that can actually be restored.
decisions.tradeoffs: A second store to secure, with its own per-tenant access rules.

risks.title: Tenant isolation rests on row-level security
risks.detail: Every tenant shares one database. A query that misses the tenant predicate, or middleware that fails to set the tenant context, exposes one customer’s HR data to another.
risks.mitigation: Tenant middleware plus RLS policies in the database, so the predicate is enforced below the application. Needs tests that attempt cross-tenant reads.

risks.title: One database for every tenant
risks.detail: A single Postgres instance is both the noisy-neighbour surface and the single point of failure, as docs/MULTI_TENANCY.md states plainly.
risks.mitigation: Accepted for the MVP with a documented migration path to schema-per-tenant.

risks.title: It holds employment data
risks.detail: Timesheets, requests and HR documents are personal data about identifiable employees, held on behalf of other companies.
risks.mitigation: Role separation is designed. Retention, export and deletion on a tenant’s behalf are not yet documented.

risks.title: Identity is a vendor
risks.detail: Auth0 pricing steps up sharply with active users, and it holds the login path for every tenant.
risks.mitigation: The adapter layer exists precisely so the provider can be replaced.

costs.notes: Priced per monthly active user once past the free tier.
